claim: DCNs are produced from a single embryonic neuroblast
source: DCNs are produced from a single embryonic neuroblast, and all express the same cell fate markers, namely the Atonal (Hassan et al., 2000) and Acj6 (see below) transcription factors.

claim: All DCNs express the Atonal transcription factor
source: DCNs are produced from a single embryonic neuroblast, and all express the same cell fate markers, namely the Atonal (Hassan et al., 2000) and Acj6 (see below) transcription factors.
evidence: Cited from Hassan et al., 2000 and shown in Figure 2A-A'

claim: All DCNs express the Acj6 transcription factor
source: DCNs are produced from a single embryonic neuroblast, and all express the same cell fate markers, namely the Atonal (Hassan et al., 2000) and Acj6 (see below) transcription factors.

claim: All postmitotic DCNs are efficiently labeled with the ato-Gal4 driver starting at the third instar larval (L3) stage
source: All postmitotic DCNs are efficiently labeled with the ato-Gal4 driver starting at the third instar larval (L3) stage (Figure 1A).

claim: DCNs innervate two regions of the optic lobes: the lobula and the medulla
source: DCNs innervate two regions of the optic lobes, the lobula and the medulla.

claim: Binary axon target choice in DCNs is a result of three distinct steps
source: This binary axon target choice is a result of three distinct steps (Srahna et al., 2006).

claim: In late third instar larvae DCN axons grow en masse toward the developing medulla neuropil attracted by a Wnt5 signal
source: First, in late third instar larvae DCN axons grow en masse toward the developing medulla neuropil attracted by a Wnt5 signal.
evidence: Referenced from previous work (Srahna et al., 2006)

claim: At 25–50 hr after puparium formation (APF), most DCN axons begin to retract back to the lobula neuropil
source: Second, at 25–50 hr after puparium formation (APF), most DCN axons begin to retract back to the lobula neuropil, likely in response to a repulsive fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signal (Figure 1A′–A″ ).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A'-A'' and referenced from previous work

claim: A small subset of regularly spaced DCN axons resist the repulsive signal and remain in the medulla
source: Third, a small subset of regularly spaced axons resist the repulsive signal, by an unknown mechanism, and remain in the medulla (Figure 1A′′′ ).

claim: There are on average 38 DCNs producing a highly stereotyped pattern of 12 spaced axons in the medulla
source: Second, although there are on average 38 DCNs producing a highly stereotyped pattern of 12 spaced axons in the medulla (Figure 2C), the DCN lineage itself is not fixed.

claim: The number of DCN neurons varies between 35–43 neurons
source: The number of neurons varies (35–43 neurons) not only between different individuals but also between the right and left sides of the same individual (r = −0.148; Figure 2D).

claim: There is no correlation between the number of neurons in a DCN cluster and the number of medulla axons it projects
source: Furthermore, there is no correlation between the number of neurons in a cluster and the number of medulla axons it projects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top graph).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top graph with r = 0.3

claim: There is no correlation between birth order and medulla vs lobula targeting
source: Thus, there is no correlation between birth order and medulla vs lobula targeting, confirming earlier observations that sibling DCN clones generated using the MARCM technique can target the medulla, the lobula, or one each (Zheng et al., 2006).
evidence: Confirmed by data in Figure 2G and cited from Zheng et al., 2006

claim: The D-V position of a DCN axon is directly and very highly correlated (r = 0.964) with the D-V position of its soma within the cluster
source: Interestingly, however, the D-V position of an axon is directly and very highly correlated (r = 0.964) with the D-V position of its soma within the cluster (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom graph) such that the most dorsal neuron gives rise to the most dorsal axon and so on (Figure 2H).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom graph

claim: DCN soma show a few sparse cells at the dorsal and ventral extremities and a majority of cells densely packed medially
source: First, DCN soma show a few sparse cells at the dorsal and ventral extremities and a majority of cells densely packed medially (Figure 3C,D).

claim: DCN medulla axons are more dense dorsally and ventrally, but more sparse medially
source: Second, DCN medulla axons are more dense dorsally and ventrally, but more sparse medially (Figure 3B).

claim: There is an inverse correlation between cell density and interaxonal distance along the D-V axis in the medulla
source: Therefore, there is an inverse correlation between cell density and interaxonal distance along the D-V axis in the medulla: four to eight medial DCN soma provide one medulla axon, whereas only one to two DCN soma target one axon to the medulla dorsally and ventrally (Figure 3E).

claim: The inverse relationship between soma density and medulla axon density is conserved in response to changes in cluster shape
source: It is crucial to note that this inverse relationship between soma density and medulla axon density is conserved in response to changes in cluster shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), yet the overall wiring pattern is preserved, strongly suggesting that DCNs use a dedicated mechanism to ensure the accuracy of the stereotyped medulla innervation pattern.

claim: DCNs express Notch and its ligand Delta during the time when DCN axon sorting is occurring (∼32 hr APF)
source: Indeed, DCNs express Notch and its ligand Delta during the time when DCN axon sorting is occurring (∼32 hr APF; Figure 4A–A‴).

claim: All DCNs express the Delta regulator Neuralized (Neur) at ∼32 hr APF
source: At this stage, all DCNs also express the Delta regulator Neuralized (Neur) and the canonical Notch pathway transcriptional reporter E(spl)-CD2 (Bailey and Posakony, 1995; Lecourtois and Schweisguth, 1995; Lai et al., 2001; Pitsouli and Delidakis, 2005; Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B and cited from multiple sources

claim: All DCNs express the canonical Notch pathway transcriptional reporter E(spl)-CD2 at ∼32 hr APF
source: At this stage, all DCNs also express the Delta regulator Neuralized (Neur) and the canonical Notch pathway transcriptional reporter E(spl)-CD2 (Bailey and Posakony, 1995; Lecourtois and Schweisguth, 1995; Lai et al., 2001; Pitsouli and Delidakis, 2005; Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B–C and cited from multiple sources

claim: Most DCNs express relatively high levels of E(spl)-CD2, whereas a minority of cells scattered across the D-V axis express relatively low levels
source: Strikingly, using anti-CD2 antibodies, we find differences in the levels of the Notch activity reporter among individual DCNs: most cells express relatively high levels of E(spl)-CD2, whereas a minority of cells scattered across the D-V axis of the cluster express relatively low levels (Figure 4D–F′).

claim: E(spl)-CD2 levels are very low in DCNs at L3
source: In contrast, E(spl)-CD2 levels are very low in DCNs at L3 (data not shown) suggesting that Notch signaling is not active in postmitotic DCNs prior to pupariation.
evidence: Stated as observation from data not shown

claim: Numb is not expressed in the DCNs
source: Finally, we do not detect expression of the asymmetric inherited Notch inhibitor Numb in the DCNs nor a phenotype with numb RNAi expression (data not shown), suggesting that differences in Notch activity between DCNs are unlikely to arise by differential inheritance, a cell fate determinant.
evidence: Stated as observation from data not shown

claim: The computational model predicts medulla targeting by a similar number and pattern of DCN axons as observed in vivo
source: The model predicts medulla targeting by a similar number and pattern of DCN axons as observed in vivo (Figure 5A red cells, Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A and 5C with in silico control 12.26 ± 2.3 SD vs in vivo control 11.88 ± 1.2 SD

claim: The computational model predicts that reduced Notch activity disrupts the stereotyped number and pattern of DCN medulla axons
source: In this case, the model predicts that the stereotyped number and pattern of DCN medulla axons are disrupted. Specifically, the medulla is targeted by an increased number of axons (17.29 ± 3.96) arising from several small clusters (2–3) of neighboring neurons, especially medially (Figure 5B, red cells and blue arrows, Figure 5C).

claim: Postmitotic, DCN-specific inhibition of Notch leads to clustered axons at several D-V positions, particularly medially
source: Postmitotic, DCN-specific inhibition of Notch or its ligands Delta and Serrate (Ser) leads to two phenotypes. First, we observe clustered axons at several D-V positions, particularly medially, as opposed to isolated single axons seen under control conditions (Figure 5D–F′,l) causing a significant decrease in axon–axon distances in the medulla (Figure 5K).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D–F′ and quantified in Figure 5K

claim: Postmitotic, DCN-specific inhibition of Notch leads to a significant increase in the number of axons targeting the medulla
source: Second, we observe a significant increase in the number of axons targeting the medulla (Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that axon clustering is the result of neighboring axons erroneously making similar target choices.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 5L showing NotchDN 17.95 ± 2.67 SD vs Control 12.33 ± 0.89 SD (p<0.001)

claim: Loss of Notch function does not alter the number of DCNs
source: Importantly, loss of Notch function alters neither the number (38.13 ± 2 SD vs 37.12 ± 3.1 SD, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) nor the expression of DCN fate markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).

claim: Loss of Notch function does not alter the expression of DCN fate markers
source: Importantly, loss of Notch function alters neither the number (38.13 ± 2 SD vs 37.12 ± 3.1 SD, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) nor the expression of DCN fate markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).

claim: RNAi knockdown of Neuralized causes clustered axons and a significant increase of medulla axons
source: RNAi knockdown of Neur, a positive regulator of Delta and Ser activity, causes clustered axons and a significant increase of medulla axons (Figure 5G,L).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5G and quantified in Figure 5L

claim: Postmitotic and DCN-specific RNAi knockdown of Su(H) and Mam result in axon clustering and a corresponding increase in medulla axon number
source: Finally, postmitotic and DCN-specific RNAi knockdown of the canonical Notch pathway nuclear effector proteins Suppressor of Hairless (Su(H)) and Mastermind (Mam) also result in axon clustering and a corresponding increase in medulla axon number (Figure 5H–J′,M).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5H–J′ and quantified in Figure 5M

claim: Gain of Pak function phenocopies Notch inhibition resulting in a significant increase and clustering of medulla axons
source: Indeed, we find that gain of Pak function, by expression of the constitutively active Pak using ato-Gal4, phenocopies Notch inhibition resulting in a significant increase and clustering of medulla axons, while knockdown of Pak levels reduces the number of medulla innervations (Figure 6A–D).

claim: Knockdown of Pak levels reduces the number of medulla innervations
source: Indeed, we find that gain of Pak function, by expression of the constitutively active Pak using ato-Gal4, phenocopies Notch inhibition resulting in a significant increase and clustering of medulla axons, while knockdown of Pak levels reduces the number of medulla innervations (Figure 6A–D).

claim: Simultaneous downregulation of JNK and Notch activities results in a phenotype similar to JNK inhibition alone
source: Simultaneous downregulation of JNK and N activities, using dominant negative transgenes driven by ato-Gal4, results in a phenotype similar to JNK inhibition alone (Figure 6D).

claim: Simultaneous reduction of both Notch activity and Pak levels results in a phenotype indistinguishable from Pak reduction alone
source: Simultaneous reduction of both Notch activity and Pak levels, using Pak RNAi, results in a phenotype indistinguishable from Pak reduction alone (Figure 6D), supporting the notion that Pak acts downstream of Notch.

claim: DCN-specific gain of Pak and loss of JNK activity shows a reduced number of medulla axons, resembling loss of JNK
source: Finally, DCN-specific gain of Pak and loss of JNK activity shows a reduced number of medulla axons, resembling loss of JNK (Figure 6D).

claim: Expression of NICD in DCNs results in a significant reduction of puc-LacZ levels
source: To this end, we expressed the constitutively active intracellular domain of Notch (NICD) in DCNs and examined the levels of JNK reporter construct puckered-LacZ (puc-LacZ; Reed et al., 2001). We found a significant reduction of puc-LacZ levels in response to Notch activation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 6F showing 3.04 ± 0.24 SD vs 1.86 ± 0.35 SD (p=0.01)

claim: Transfection of DmBG2-c3 cells with NICD results in a significant decrease in both Pak and pJNK levels
source: Next, we transfected the Drosophila neuronal cell line DmBG2-c3 with NICD and assayed the effects on Pak and phospho-JNK (active JNK) levels. This resulted in a significant decrease in both Pak and pJNK levels, consistent with our in vivo observations (Figure 6G).

claim: Reduction of Notch activity at the restrictive temperature results in clusters of neighboring axons in the medulla and a significant increase in the number of medulla axons
source: Reduction of Notch activity at the restrictive temperature results in clusters of neighboring axons in the medulla and a significant increase in the number of medulla axons (Figure 7A–E).

claim: Decreasing Notch activity only alters axon target choice between 24 and 60 hr APF, but neither before nor after
source: Decreasing Notch activity only alters axon target choice between 24 and 60 hr APF, but neither before nor after (Figure 7B,E).

claim: Inhibition of Notch function specifically within the DCNs only during pupal development results in a very similar phenotype to temperature shift experiments
source: Importantly, inhibition of Notch function specifically within the DCNs only during pupal development, using a combination of ato-Gal4 and a temperature-sensitive Gal80 (McGuire et al., 2003), results in a very similar phenotype (Figure 7E′).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 7E′ and cited from McGuire et al., 2003

claim: Gain of Notch function via DCN-specific expression of NICD or Su(H) strongly reduces the number of medulla axons found in the adult brain
source: Finally, gain of Notch function via DCN-specific expression of NICD or Su(H) strongly reduces the number of medulla axons found in the adult brain, but, importantly, does not inhibit their initial outgrowth into the medulla (Figure 7F–J), confirming that canonical Notch signaling specifically regulates the ability of axons to remain in the medulla after initial targeting.

claim: Gain of Notch function does not inhibit initial DCN axon outgrowth into the medulla
source: Finally, gain of Notch function via DCN-specific expression of NICD or Su(H) strongly reduces the number of medulla axons found in the adult brain, but, importantly, does not inhibit their initial outgrowth into the medulla (Figure 7F–J), confirming that canonical Notch signaling specifically regulates the ability of axons to remain in the medulla after initial targeting.

claim: Only 24% of control single cell clones target the medulla
source: We found that whereas only 24% of the control clones target the medulla, approximately 60% of all Notch mutant clones—both null and DN—do so, with the most pronounced effect occurring medially (p<0.001 null, p<0.001 DN, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 8B–D).

claim: Approximately 60% of all Notch mutant single cell clones target the medulla
source: We found that whereas only 24% of the control clones target the medulla, approximately 60% of all Notch mutant clones—both null and DN—do so, with the most pronounced effect occurring medially (p<0.001 null, p<0.001 DN, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 8B–D).

claim: Notch signaling levels autonomously regulate the axon target choice of individual DCNs
source: Therefore, Notch signaling levels autonomously regulate the axon target choice of individual DCNs.
evidence: Inferred from single cell MARCM experiments shown in Figure 8B–D

claim: The overall number and pattern of medulla axons in single Notch mutant clones is indistinguishable from control
source: Analysis of the number, clustering, and spatial pattern of medulla axons in these clones show that the Notch mutant axon remains correctly spaced and the overall number and pattern of axons in the medulla is indistinguishable from control (Figure 8E′,F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8E′,F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: 87% (20/23) of single Notch mutant axons are within the normal spacing range
source: Next, we analyzed 23 axon–axon distances representing 12 individual mutant clones and compared them to the distances observed in controls. We found that 87% (20/23) of the mutant axons are within the normal range, as expected if neighboring control neurons innervate the lobula (Figure 8G).

claim: The biased medulla innervation caused by loss of Notch activity does not alter the D-V positional relationship between neuronal soma and axon
source: Crucially, the biased medulla innervation caused by loss of Notch activity does not alter the D-V positional relationship between neuronal soma and axon; dorsal neurons still project dorsally, medial neurons project medially, and ventral neurons project ventrally (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: In 45% of multi-cell Notch mutant clones (20/44), axon clustering is observed
source: Second, in 45% of the clones (20/44), in addition to mutant axons targeting the medulla (Figure 8I′, white arrows), axon clustering is observed (p=0.0094 Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Quantified from experiments shown in Figure 8I

claim: Multi-cell Notch mutant clones show a significantly increased number of medulla axons
source: Furthermore, the number of medulla axons is significantly increased, and the axon–axon distances within these clones is drastically reduced (Figure 8I–K and Figure 8—figure supplement 3), suggesting that in these cases interacting neurons of one subcluster have been targeted by the stochastic inhibition of Notch.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 8J showing multicell loss of Notch function clones 13.65 ± 1.09 SD vs multicell control clones 11.6 ± 1.19 SD (p<0.001)

claim: Axon–axon distances within multi-cell Notch mutant clones is drastically reduced
source: Furthermore, the number of medulla axons is significantly increased, and the axon–axon distances within these clones is drastically reduced (Figure 8I–K and Figure 8—figure supplement 3), suggesting that in these cases interacting neurons of one subcluster have been targeted by the stochastic inhibition of Notch.

claim: Mutual inhibition among postmitotic neurons regulates the robustness of axon target choice in DCNs
source: We show that during the development of the Drosophila central nervous system, mutual inhibition among groups of neighboring postmitotic neurons during development regulates the robustness of axon target choice in a nondeterministic neuronal circuit.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript

claim: Neighboring postmitotic neurons communicate through Notch signaling during axonal targeting to ensure balanced alternative axon target choices without a corresponding change in cell fate
source: Specifically, neighboring postmitotic neurons communicate through Notch signaling during axonal targeting, to ensure balanced alternative axon target choices without a corresponding change in cell fate.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing Notch signaling affects axon targeting but not cell fate markers

claim: Loss of Notch in postmitotic neurons modulates an axon's target choice
source: Loss of Notch in postmitotic neurons modulates an axon's target choice.
evidence: Shown by single cell MARCM experiments in Figure 8

claim: When a single neuron loses Notch function, neighboring axons respond by choosing the complementary target, preserving the stereotyped connectivity pattern
source: However, because neighboring axons respond by choosing the complementary target, the stereotyped connectivity pattern is preserved.
evidence: Shown by single cell MARCM experiments in Figure 8E-G

claim: Loss of Notch in clones of neighboring postmitotic neurons results in erroneous coinnervation by multiple axons
source: In contrast, loss of Notch in clones of neighboring postmitotic neurons results in erroneous coinnervation by multiple axons.
evidence: Shown by multi-cell clone experiments in Figure 8H-K

claim: Notch signaling has a novel cell fate independent function in axonal targeting
source: Our observations establish mutual inhibition of axonal target choice as a robustness mechanism for brain wiring and unveil a novel cell fate independent function for canonical Notch signaling.
evidence: Supported by data showing Notch affects axon targeting without changing cell fate markers

claim: The most well-established function for Notch signaling in neural development is the selection of neural progenitor cells through mutual or lateral inhibition
source: The most well-established function for Notch signaling in neural development is the selection of neural progenitor cells through a process termed mutual or lateral inhibition (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 1999).

claim: A second important function for Notch signaling is the establishment of alternate binary cell fates of sibling neurons
source: A second important function for Notch signaling is the establishment of alternate binary cell fates of sibling neurons.

claim: Binary cell fate specification via Notch requires the asymmetric inheritance of the Notch antagonist Numb by one of the two sibling neurons in a terminal cell division
source: In contrast to lateral inhibition, this function requires the asymmetric inheritance of the Notch antagonist Numb by one of the two sibling neurons in a terminal cell division (Guo et al., 1996; Spana and Doe, 1996; Knoblich, 1997).
evidence: Cited from Guo et al., 1996; Spana and Doe, 1996; Knoblich, 1997

claim: In the fly visual system, R7 and R8 photoreceptors independently require Notch activity to be specified
source: In the fly visual system, the R7 and R8 photoreceptors, which independently require Notch activity to be specified, make alternative axonal target choices that appear to be consequences of their different fates.

claim: The canonical fate marker transcription factors Prospero and Senseless are required for differential targeting of R7 and R8 photoreceptors
source: Indeed, their canonical fate marker transcription factors Prospero and Senseless, respectively, are required for this differential targeting (Morey et al., 2008).

claim: In the olfactory system of Drosophila, sibling neurons target their axon to different CNS glomeruli due to differential cell fate specification
source: In the olfactory system of Drosophila, sibling neurons target their axon to different central nervous system (CNS) glomeruli due to differential cell fate specification (Endo et al., 2007).

claim: Chromatin modification of Notch targets by the Hamlet protein diversifies cell fate and axonal targeting in olfactory neurons
source: A recent elegant extension of this work shows that chromatin modification of Notch targets by the Hamlet protein further diversifies cell fate and axonal targeting in olfactory neurons (Endo et al., 2012).

claim: There are more diverse wiring morphologies in CNS neurons than can be accounted for by the number of cell types
source: Finally, an extensive analysis of CNS neurons in the fly olfactory circuit shows that there are more diverse wiring morphologies than can be accounted for by the number of cell types (Chou et al., 2010), suggesting that post-fate mechanisms may be crucial in wiring the Drosophila CNS.

claim: DCNs are a group of bilateral commissural higher order neurons in the visual system of Drosophila
source: Here we show that the dorsal cluster neurons (DCNs), a group of bilateral commissural higher order neurons in the visual system of Drosophila (Hassan et al., 2000) are intrinsically variable in number within and between individuals, yet generate a highly stereotyped wiring diagram.

claim: DCNs are intrinsically variable in number within and between individuals, yet generate a highly stereotyped wiring diagram
source: Here we show that the dorsal cluster neurons (DCNs), a group of bilateral commissural higher order neurons in the visual system of Drosophila (Hassan et al., 2000) are intrinsically variable in number within and between individuals, yet generate a highly stereotyped wiring diagram.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analyses in Figure 2

claim: Notch-mediated mutual inhibition acts late in development on postmitotic neurons to bias axonal target choice
source: We combine high resolution quantitative anatomical analyses, computational modeling, and genetic dissection to show that Notch-mediated mutual inhibition acts late in development on postmitotic neurons to bias axonal target choice.
evidence: Demonstrated by temporal experiments in Figure 7

claim: Notch-mediated mutual inhibition ensures the reproducibility of the DCN connectivity pattern
source: Finally, we show that this mechanism ensures the reproducibility of the DCN connectivity pattern.
evidence: Demonstrated by single and multi-cell clone experiments in Figure 8

claim: Wnt and FGF have opposing effects on JNK activity in DCNs
source: Wnt and FGF have opposing effects on Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) activity, which is both necessary and sufficient for DCN axon growth.
evidence: Referenced from previous work (Srahna et al., 2006)

claim: JNK activity is both necessary and sufficient for DCN axon growth
source: Wnt and FGF have opposing effects on Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) activity, which is both necessary and sufficient for DCN axon growth.
evidence: Referenced from previous work (Srahna et al., 2006)

claim: Notch reduces JNK activity via inhibition of Pak function
source: These data support a model whereby N reduces JNK activity via inhibition of Pak function (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction experiments in Figure 6

claim: Notch activity sets the baseline JNK activity threshold which distinguishes medulla-targeting from lobula-targeting neurons
source: Together, these data suggest that Notch activity sets the baseline JNK activity threshold which distinguishes medulla-targeting from lobula-targeting neurons (Figure 6E).
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction experiments in Figure 6

claim: The decision to target the medulla neuropil of single cell Notch null mutant clone is probabilistic (∼60%) rather than absolute (100%)
source: First, the decision to target the medulla neuropil of single cell Notch null mutant clone is probabilistic (∼60%) rather than absolute (100%) as would be expected for cell fate specification.

claim: The requirement for Notch signaling in establishing the wiring diagram is restricted to 24–60 hr APF
source: Second, the requirement for Notch signaling in establishing the wiring diagram is restricted to 24–60 hr APF, and third, Notch signaling affects neither the lineage size nor the expression of different cell fate markers in the DCNs early in development.

claim: During adult brain development, ato-Gal4 is only active in DCNs postmitotically and after their axons begin to grow
source: It is critical to note that during adult brain development, ato-Gal4 is only active in DCNs postmitotically and after their axons begin to grow (Hassan et al., 2000; Srahna et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Hassan et al., 2000; Srahna et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2006

claim: Medulla vs lobula axon target choice can be viewed as a form of sub-fate choice
source: It should be noted that medulla vs lobula axon target choice can be viewed as a form of sub-fate choice.

claim: The 'sub-fate' of medulla vs lobula targeting is not a cell-autonomous translation of birth order instructions, but is subject to regulation by the choices of neighboring cells
source: The important discovery here is that this 'sub-fate' is not a cell-autonomous translation of birth order instructions, but is rather subject to regulation by the choices of neighboring cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing no correlation with birth order and compensation by neighboring cells

claim: The inhibitory interactions in DCNs are likely taking place between the neuronal cell bodies
source: It is likely that the inhibitory interactions are taking place between the neuronal cell bodies, especially given the requirement for the nuclear factors Su(H) and Mam and the effects on the E(spl) transcriptional reporter.
evidence: Inferred from requirement of nuclear factors and transcriptional reporter

claim: Interactions between axons prior to or shortly after their defasciculation within the medulla cannot be formally ruled out
source: However, interactions between axons prior to or shortly after their defasciculation within the medulla cannot be formally ruled out.

claim: Lateral inhibition among postmitotic neurons is a novel mechanism for brain wiring
source: Here, we report lateral inhibition as a novel mechanism for brain wiring.

claim: Axonal target choice resulting from mutual inhibition by neighboring postmitotic neurons is an additional layer of regulation that complements, but is independent of, traditional axon guidance cues
source: Axonal target choice resulting from mutual inhibition by neighboring postmitotic neurons is interesting, not only as a novel function for Notch signaling but also as an additional layer of regulation that complements, but is independent of, traditional axon guidance cues.

claim: A degree of circuit-level plasticity is a more useful strategy in higher order brain centers than strict coupling of fate to targeting
source: While it may be sensible for sensory neurons to couple fate to targeting so that the same sensory information is carried by the same type of neuron in different animals, it is reasonable to speculate that a degree of circuit-level plasticity is a more useful strategy in higher order brain centers, where meaningful information is likely to be encoded at the network level and not by single cells.

claim: A mechanism that ensures the reproducibility of the connectivity pattern of an entire circuit would be evolutionarily favored over a mechanism that risks the population connectivity pattern in favor of attempting to generate the same connectivity of precisely the same cell
source: Finally, given the inevitable and significant genetic and environmental variability in the real world, it seems rather intuitive that a mechanism that ensures the reproducibility of the connectivity pattern of an entire circuit, would be evolutionarily favored over a mechanisms that would risk the population connectivity pattern in favor of attempting to generate the same connectivity of precisely the same cell.
